## The Setup

Another classic dataset to illustrate IV concept was introduced in Card (1995).
There it was used to study the impact of (college) education on wages using whether the
observation lives close to a college as an instrument for (college) education.
An important characteristics of the setup is that the instrument is
unconditionally most likely not randomly assigned.

We consider a binarized version of the treatment, i.e. we consider an
observation as treated if here education in the dataset is recorded as at least
13 years. The treatment can therefore be viewed as _some college_.

This is in line with modern takes at the dataset such as Sloczynski (2021) and Tübbicke (2023). 

The dataset consists of 3010 men
from the 1976 National Longitudinal Survey of Young
Men. The instrument `nearc4` indicates whether a man grew up in a local labour
market with a four-year college, and the outcome `lwage` is the log wage.

In @lst-card-sample, we follow Sloczynski (2021) and Tübbicke (2023) in restricting the sample to
covariate cells with at least five observations. A  cell is one of the
observed combinations of `black`, `south66`, `south`, `smsa66` and `smsa`.
This drops 22 observations and leaves 2988.

```{python}
#| label: lst-card-sample
#| code-summary: "Show code (estimation sample)"
#| code-fold: false
import polars as pl

from qte.datasets import load_card

CARD_CELLS = ["black", "south66", "south", "smsa66", "smsa"]
CARD_COVARIATES = (
    "exper + expersq + black + south + smsa + smsa66 "
    "+ reg662 + reg663 + reg664 + reg665 + reg666 + reg667 + reg668 + reg669"
)

sample = load_card(treatment_cutoff=13)
card = sample.filter(pl.len().over(CARD_CELLS) >= 5)
print(f"{sample.height} observations, {sample.height - card.height} dropped, {card.height} left")
```

## Descriptive Statistics

@lst-card-data shows how to generate descriptive statistics for the dataset by instrument value, treatment status and for the entire dataset using the `make_descriptive_statistics` function from `py-qte`. @tbl-card-data shows th results.

```{python}
#| label: lst-card-data
#| code-summary: "Show code (Generation of descriptive statistics)"
#| code-fold: false
from qte.iv.descriptives import make_descriptive_statistics

t_desc=make_descriptive_statistics(
    card,
    "lwage",
    "college",
    "nearc4",
    covariates=["exper", "educ", "age", "black", "smsa", "south"],
    labels={
        "lwage": "Log wage",
        "college": "College",
        "exper": "Experience",
        "educ": "Years of education",
        "age": "Age",
        "black": "Black",
        "smsa": "SMSA",
        "south": "South",
    },
    title="Table 1. Card Data, Means and Standard Deviations",
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-card-data
#| code-summary: "Show code (Card descriptive statistics)"
t_desc
```

@tbl-card-data reveals large differences across instrument values in most
covariates that are also statistically significant. One can, therefore, not
assume that the instrument is (as good as) randomly assigned and the analysis
should condition any first stage on covariates.

## Unconditional Local QTE

In @lst-card-estimate, we estimate unconditional local treatment effects using
the `estimate_unconditional_local_effects` function from `py-qte`. We consider
a large number of boostrap replication to estimate the standard error. The
result object returned by `estimate_unconditional_local_effects` carries its
own presentation methods: `plot` for the figure and `tabulate` for the table,
both generated in @lst-card-estimate and shown side by side in @fig-card-plot.

```{python}
#| label: lst-card-estimate
#| code-summary: "Show code (local QTE on the Card data)"
#| code-fold: false
with timer("card"):
    card_res = estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
        card,
        "lwage",
        "college",
        "nearc4",
        qs=[0.1, 0.5, 0.9],
        instrument_probability_formula=CARD_COVARIATES,
        estimator=Estimator.SIGNED,
        bootstrap_config=BootstrapConfig(n_iter=1000, seed=42, n_workers=4),
    )

card_fig = card_res.plot()
card_tbl = card_res.tabulate(quantiles=REPORT)
```

@fig-card-plot reports the results.


```{python}
#| label: fig-card-plot
#| code-summary: "Show code (plot and table side by side)"
#| fig-cap: "Local quantile treatment effects on the Card data."
import vl_convert as vlc
from IPython.display import publish_display_data

plot_svg = vlc.vegalite_to_svg(card_fig.to_dict())
table_html = card_tbl.as_raw_html()
publish_display_data(
    {"text/html": f'<div class="iv-side"><div>{plot_svg}</div><div>{table_html}</div></div>'}
)
```

For the mean, the results are quite close to the results reported by Tübbicke
(2023) both in terms of the point estimates and in terms of the standard error.
Notice that for the mean these results suggest that (some) college education
increases income by about 35% (for the compliers). This effect is quite imprecisely measured. The point estiamte is much larger than the OLS esimate which is about 20% in Tuebbicke (2023) but a lot smaller than the 2SLS estimate reported in Tuebbicke (2023) which translate into a somewhat difficult beliefe effect of about 80% of some college education on mean income. The results also suggest that there is not much effect heterogeneity in terms of the quantiles
